source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Gap 1. Retrieval-augmented, fine-tuned GPT-4 forecaster tested on questions resolved after model cut-offs. Raw models are poor forecasters; the system nears but does not beat the crowd. It reports Brier and calibration of the stated probability, but no AUROC of the stated confidence.
numbers: Test set Brier: system .179 vs human crowd .149; accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Random guessing .25. Zero-shot best base model (GPT-4-1106) .208; most models around or worse than .25. Reported RMS calibration error .42 (system) vs .38 (crowd) as printed. Where the crowd is uncertain the system scores .240 vs .247.
limits: The output is a forecast probability, not a verbal confidence in a chosen answer. 2023-24 models. The RMS calibration figures are printed as .42 and .38, which look like a different scale from Brier; quoted as the paper states them.
agent_relevance: A scaffolded forecaster can be calibrated on real, later-resolving questions, but retrieval, fine-tuning and ensembling did the work, not one stated confidence. Frontier 2026 AUROC on resolving questions is still unmeasured here.

source: Karger et al. (2024) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Gap 1. A benchmark of 1,000 auto-generated, regularly updated future-event questions, built so no answer exists at submission. Expert forecasters beat the top LLM.
numbers: N=200 random subset compared across experts, public and LLMs; expert vs top LLM p<0.001.
limits: Abstract page only (full paper not opened). Reports forecast skill, not discrimination of stated confidence.
agent_relevance: The right kind of test bed for gap 1 (leak-free, resolving questions). A 2026 stated-confidence AUROC check should run here, not on trivia.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Bastos, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Gap 1. A crowd of 12 LLMs matched a human tournament crowd on binary questions. Single LLMs leaned above 50% (acquiescence) though resolutions were near even.
numbers: Study 1: 12 LLMs, 31 binary questions, 925 human forecasters; LLM crowd not different from human crowd. Study 2: showing the human median to GPT-4 and Claude 2 raised accuracy 17-28%, still worse than averaging human and machine.
limits: Abstract page only. Small question set (31). Old models.
agent_relevance: Averaging across independent samples fixes a single-sample bias on real forecasts. Supports ensemble agreement over one stated confidence, and a base-rate check against yes-bias.

finding: Gaps 3 and 5. 15 frontier models, verbalized confidence scored by Brier on 200 private multiple-choice questions. Best frontier models beat the calibrated-random baseline; the weakest does not. More reasoning effort gives better Brier in one family.
numbers: Brier: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview both 0.103; calibrated-random 0.1875; Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite 0.367; 5 of 15 models worse than the 0.1875 baseline. Most accurate model (Gemini 3.1 Pro, 82.7%) not best calibrated. GPT-5 reasoning effort: Standard 0.117, High 0.121, Low 0.141. Human tester Brier 0.105 (accuracy 70.5%). Unknowable category: models default to a 25% floor even when right more often.
limits: Only 200 multiple-choice items, 3 runs at temperature 1.0; private set; preprint. Brier only, no AUROC. Reasoning effort varied in one family only.
agent_relevance: Frontier models do use low values and are not stuck at 95%+: saturation is a small-model problem. Calibration differs widely by model, so the guardrail must measure, not assume. A 25% floor is a known habit.

source: Ghosh, Kumar, Garg (2026) Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in LLMs
finding: Gap 2. Pre-registered audit of Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B on PopQA, SimpleQA, GSM8K, MATH. Verbal confidence has good ECE but little sorting power; 10-sample agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution and the best Brier.
numbers: Matched N=842. Brier: verbal .1713, internal probe .1524, behavioral consensus (10 samples, T=0.8) .1465. Resolution: .0316 verbal, .0516 probe, .0637 consensus (2.02x). ECE (15 bins): .0366, .0500, .0704. Pooled ECE verbal .0356 vs behavioral .0427 vs internal .0368, indistinguishable.
limits: Small open models (0.5-7B), not frontier. 10 samples, so cost is far above one stated confidence. Preprint. A prompt-only TF-IDF classifier matched the probe in most retrieval cells.
agent_relevance: Direct support: report resolution or AUROC, never ECE alone. Agreement across samples sorts right from wrong better than one stated number, but costs 10 calls.

source: Boubnovski Martell et al. (2026) Measuring Black-Box Confidence via Reasoning Trajectories
finding: Gap 2. On frontier reasoners (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6) a trace-geometry plus coverage plus verbalization score at 4 samples beats self-consistency at 8 samples, at about half the cost of SC at 10.
numbers: MedQA-USMLE, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, 6 settings: median AUC 0.78 vs 0.71 (+0.075) for K=4 fusion vs SC@8, better in 6/6. Near-tie: SC 0.747 vs 0.727 in one setting. Cost per question: SC@10 $0.2839 vs fusion@4 $0.1379 (51.4% saving; 42.6-54.4% by setting). Fusion beat the best single channel in 17/18 settings, max AUC 0.92.
limits: The score needs an embedder and a judge call, not a plain stated confidence. Multiple-choice benchmarks, about 200 items each. Preprint. Not the exact comparison asked (SC vs one sample plus verification).
agent_relevance: At comparable cost a trace-based or judged signal can beat plain agreement, so raw agreement is a strong baseline but not the ceiling. Judging the trace is worth testing.

source: Boubnovski Martell et al. (2026) verbalization channel audit (Table 15, appendix D.5)
finding: Gaps 1 and 2. Standalone verbalized-confidence AUC on frontier reasoners is fair on hard multiple-choice sets and adds little over trace geometry in most settings.
numbers: Verbalized AUC (accuracy): MedQA/Gemini .751 (.805); MedQA/Claude .787 (.744); GPQA/Gemini .628 (.653); GPQA/Claude .580 (.508); MMLU-Pro/Gemini .633 (.800); MMLU-Pro/Claude .738 (.725). Gain from adding V over geometry: +0.002 to +0.112. V adds signal in only 6/18 open-ended settings. Spearman of AUC(V) with accuracy +0.71 (N=6, p=0.11).
limits: Six settings, closed-set questions with known answers, not forecasts. Numeric self-rating at the end of the trace.
agent_relevance: Frontier verbal AUROC on knowledge questions ranges 0.58-0.79; only 3 of 6 are above 0.7. A 0.7 threshold on open forecasting questions is not safe to assume. Pair stated confidence with a second signal.

source: Ghosh, Kumar, Garg (2026) verbal format instability (Table 2)
finding: Gap 3. Three verbal formats (numeric, labelled levels, answer-or-pass with scoring +1/-2/0) barely correlate. The numeric format is at ceiling, yet the model still passes often when penalties are explicit.
numbers: Spearman between formats: A-B +0.126, A-C -0.069 (CI -0.111 to -0.030), B-C +0.247; all below the pre-registered 0.60. Format A: 13,121 of 15,000 responses state 90 or more; among those, the model passed in Format C 26.8% of the time. Base model verbal confidence degenerate.
limits: Qwen2.5 0.5-7B only. Format B is labels mapped to probabilities by a fixed table; not a frontier test.
agent_relevance: The bin vocabulary changes the signal a lot, and one model ranks items differently across formats. A fixed 5-bin scheme must be validated on its own. Small models saturate; this does not show frontier models do.

source: Wang et al. (2026) On the Pitfalls of Verbalized Confidence Priors for Calibrating Large Reasoning Models
finding: Gap 3. Open reasoning models (Qwen3-8B, Gemma4-E2B, OLMo3-7B) put almost all confidence mass on a few high values, for wrong answers too. The concentration survives RLCR training. A calibrated prior added by supervised fine-tuning helps exploration.
numbers: Fewer than 5% of responses below confidence 0.5 in all three models; figure labels give 1.64% (Gemma4-E2B) and 4.90% (OLMo3-7B). Tested on 16 math and reasoning benchmarks with five RL algorithms.
limits: Preprint, open 7-8B reasoning models only. Frontier closed models not tested. Percentages read from figure labels in the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Saturation also affects mid-size reasoning models, so a 5-bin vocabulary will likely collapse into the top one or two bins for them. Count bin use before trusting a bin label.

source: Kumaran (2026) Reported Confidence in LLMs Tracks Commitment More Than Correctness
finding: Gap 4. In a two-stage task (answer with confidence, then commit or abstain) verbal confidence predicts the later abstain decision much better than it predicts correctness. Calibrated log-probs do not show this gap. Residual verbal confidence has no correctness signal.
numbers: Median AUROC gap (abstention minus correctness) +0.16 over 4 non-reasoning and 4 reasoning models on 4 benchmarks. Class-VC gap above threshold in 7/8 cells (median +0.13, p=0.008); Num-VC 6/7 cells (median +0.20, p=0.039); log-prob gap median +0.018 (2/8 cells). After removing the log-prob part, residual VC correctness AUROC mean 0.473 vs 0.686 for residual log-prob. Gemma 4: later decision decodable from activations at AUROC 0.94 vs 0.66 for correctness; steering shifted abstention.
limits: Single author, preprint. Mechanistic part on Gemma 3 and 4 only. Abstention is the model own choice, not an externally priced penalty.
agent_relevance: A stated confidence is partly a commitment signal. An abstain rule driven by it will be consistent but not necessarily accurate. Gate abstention on an outcome-grounded signal as well.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (cross-read against d08 and d10; not re-opened)
finding: Gap 4. Not newly opened this pass. Earlier file c22 reports that models almost never abstain under penalties. Ghosh (d08) found passes even at 90+ stated confidence in small models under +1/-2/0 scoring. Set-ups differ.
numbers: See c22. Ghosh 2026: 26.8% pass among the 13,121 responses stating 90 or more.
limits: The two sources differ in model size and set-up and are not reconciled. opened:false for this line.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that an abstain rule driven by stated confidence raises utility. Needs an own test with an expected-utility measure. Gap 4 stays open.

source: Saenko, Gajjar, Ganiyu, Shah (2026) Twin-Pass CoT-Ensembling for Telco LLMs
finding: Gaps 5 and 8. Prompt-only: after answering, run separate blind passes where the model rates its own reasoning 1-5, then average. This cuts ECE in Gemma-3 models, most for the smallest.
numbers: ECE raw to mean-of-passes: TeleQnA Gemma-3-4B 0.400 to 0.108 (+73.0%), 12B 0.314 to 0.244 (+22.2%), 27B 0.255 to 0.172 (+32.5%). ORANBench 4B 0.800 to 0.093 (+88.4%), 12B 0.318 to 0.249 (+21.6%), 27B 0.252 to 0.208 (+17.3%). Accuracy 0.685-0.747. Tier rule: score 4.5-5 bypasses review, below 3 escalates.
limits: Gemma-3 only, telecom multiple choice, N 150-1,000 for 4B and 27B. ECE only; no AUROC read. 4B baseline ECE (0.8) is extreme. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Confidence rated in a separate blind pass beats confidence stated in the same pass as the answer. It is a prompt-only gain, but it shrinks with model size (17-33% at 27B), so the frontier effect is unproven.

source: Miao and Ungar (2026) Closing the Confidence-Faithfulness Gap in LLMs
finding: Gap 5. In three open models, reasoning in the same prompt as the confidence report disrupts the confidence direction ("Reasoning Contamination"). Calibration and verbalized confidence are encoded in nearly orthogonal directions.
numbers: Cosine between accuracy and confidence directions: under 0.04 in Qwen-2.5-7B-Base; under the pure-confidence prompt +0.26, under a joint solve-and-rate prompt -0.63. Held across three open-weight models and four datasets.
limits: Probing and steering on open 7B-class models; no frontier or API reasoning models. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Asking for confidence in the same breath as the reasoning may hurt. A separate rating step after the answer (d12) fits this. The before-versus-after test is still not run on frontier models.

source: Fang, Zhao, Wang, Cheng (2026) REHEARSE: Experiential Rehearsal for Verbal Confidence Calibration
finding: Gap 8. Training-free: the model plays a scored credence game under a strictly proper rule, a short summary of its over- or under-confidence goes into the prompt, and it applies this when answering. Reduces ECE without changing weights.
numbers: Average ECE down 58% relative to the uncalibrated baseline over 4 LLMs, 3 benchmarks, 5 seeds (12 model-dataset cells); up to 0.727 ECE reduction in one cell. Best on Acc, ECE, Brier; the FaR baseline edges it on AUROC. For comparison RLCR in-domain ECE 0.37 to 0.03 (c20).
limits: Preprint under review. Needs a pre-game of about 50 scored rounds. One cell shows accuracy 0.128 to 0.822 for LLaMA-3.1-8B, which suggests a format fix rather than calibration. Reported AUROC gain is small.
agent_relevance: A prompt-level route recovers part of the ECE gain but not clearly the sorting power. No prompt-only method is yet shown to match RLCR on AUROC. A scored-feedback prefix is cheap to test in our scaffold.

source: Zong et al. (2025) CritiCal: Can Critique Help LLM Uncertainty or Confidence Calibration?
finding: Gap 7. Plain supervised fine-tuning on confidence labels does not transfer to out-of-distribution data. Training on critiques transfers somewhat better, from StrategyQA to MATH-Perturb.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, confidence, StrategyQA to MATH-Perturb. SFT_Soft ECE 0.611 in-distribution to 0.625 out (AUROC 0.562 to 0.578); SFT_Hard out ECE 0.610, AUROC 0.542; CritiCal ECE 0.588 in, 0.571 out (AUROC 0.593 both).
limits: Requires training. Gains are small (ECE 0.04-0.05) and absolute ECE stays near 0.6. 7B models. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Calibration learned on one task does not travel freely. A prompt-only guardrail should be re-checked per task type, not tuned once.

source: Tan, Lin, Motani, Lee (2026) On the Effectiveness of Reward Functions in RL for Confidence Calibration
finding: Gap 8. RL with separate rewards for confidence on correct and on wrong answers can be hacked: the model may answer wrong on purpose to look calibrated. Non-hackable schemes exist.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read; selective confidence reward hacking shown on practical datasets under hackable schemes. No headline number recorded.
limits: Only the opening read in depth. Preprint. About training, not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: Training-based calibration (RLCR-like) has its own failure mode. For a scaffold with no training, prefer measurement and abstain rules over reward shaping.

source: Moore and Healy (2008) The Trouble with Overconfidence (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Gap 9, partial. Overestimation of own performance, overplacement against others and overprecision are different things. Overestimation and overplacement reverse between hard and easy tasks; overprecision is more persistent.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. Hard tasks: people overestimate performance but think they are worse than others. Easy tasks: the reverse.
limits: Abstract only; full paper not read. Lichtenstein et al. 1982 (DTIC ADA101986) and Wallsten et al. 1986 (DTIC ADA196944) were located by DOI but the PDF fetch was blocked (HTTP 403, HTML page). Original numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: The hard-easy effect means one overconfidence guardrail is wrong for easy items: do not push confidence down blindly. For LLMs it is an analogy only; no direct LLM test here.
